p:
Hold on, I will say we had– if I recall correctly, and I wish that you– that I knew that this was going to come up, I would have brought the specifics of that incident, but my recollection is that she was brought to the hospital

and was released from the hospital and put back in our custody.
Yes.
Okay.
And what was the open warrant for? And also, what's the policy when it comes to people or individuals who might be pregnant or have medical—

Yeah, so, Chair, you know, what we will do is we will follow up with you in writing about both the particulars of what occurred, and we can also provide you with any applicable policies. We didn't— we did not come prepared today to talk about those specifics of this, and I—

[interposing] Hold on. The Chief of Department can speak about policy, the policies, but what I don't want to do is talk in an open forum about a specific individual and a specific case. So go ahead with the policy.

So the policy is to bring that individual to the hospital, which the policy was

followed. The hospital then released that individual back to our custody.
Okay, and what was the open warrant for?
Again, I don't wanna discuss a specific individual's case in an open setting like this.

Okay. So, a few questions— a few final questions. I know earlier you mentioned there's a new precinct in the Borough of Queens. What are factors that you take into consideration when determining whether to build a new precinct? I'm only asking because I know that some— a few precincts in the Bronx are—
[interposing] Lots of things. The geographical size of the precinct, response times, 911 calls, 311 calls, crime conditions. There is a lot that goes into it.

Okay. All right. And last but not least, you know, we've obviously made a lot of progress on the issue of safety. As we know, crime has gone down for the most part, shootings murders, and etcetera. What would you say are the

top three things that have helped us get there? Police presence, technology, I'm sure also– in your opinion what would be three things that stand out on that?

Could have listed one more and you would have answered the question yourself. You were doing great. I give a lot of credit to the Chief of Department and the Chief of Crime Control's precision policing strategies, not just the zones. What happens is when we see a crime problem, we look at the data and we come up with a very specific data-driven response to it. We have, for example, one response based on the data that we saw to retail theft. Retail theft is down. Another data-driven strategy to burglaries. Burglaries we then came— we saw come down. Same thing for shooting incidents and shooting victims. So I would say largely it has been precision policing, which to my mind is data-driven strategies to address specific types of crime that we see. Second, I agree with you, the technology has been extremely helpful in our efforts. And third, and I think most importantly, our cops are doing incredible work. They are out there

every day. They are engaged. They are carrying out the strategies that we have given them with a lot of nobility and a lot of professionalism. And without their work, we would not see any of the reductions that we are enjoying today. Thank you.

Thank you. And the final question is on the unsafe use of mobility devices. As we know, mobility devices such as e-bikes, scooters, mopeds, they're good. You could easily move around. They reduce traffic. They also reduce air pollution versus, for example, using cars. But we have seen people use them in an unsafe way. And of course, very complex issue. It could be super difficult to enforce the rules. You stop them, they could easily take off, and it's difficult to, you know, engage in a high vehicle pursuit. And also they could obviously move much faster than other cars and enter areas that cars can't enter. Do you think the reckless use of these items are a problem? And if yes, what's the policy on this?

So yes, I think it's a problem, and I think that the data bears it out. I want to be clear that for reckless driving of these,

you know, smaller mobility devices, we still today can issue criminal summonses for that, and we continue to issue criminal summonses for reckless use of e-bikes and scooters. But for other offenses, like, for example, speeding or running a red light, things that come just short of recklessness, we— or the legal definition of recklessness— we have reverted from issuing C summonses to issuing B summonses based on conversations with City Hall.
All right, thank you for the information. I know my colleagues have a second round of questions, so I'll pause here. Thank you.
Thank you.

Okay, Council Member Cabán followed by Wong. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Thank you. For my questions, I just want to address a couple things. The woman who gave birth in cuffs in the courthouse in Brooklyn, and I'm going to say that because the cuffs were taken off when the baby was crowning. And any mother will tell you that labor and birth is much more and much longer than those final few moments of

when your baby crowns and is actually born. So I would suggest that whoever's giving y'all that line, whoever's working on the PR spin, rethink that one, because that is a terrible answer. I'm emotional just like even– I can't believe that that was the answer that was given. I did wanna correct the record. I know that there was a– it was testified to that the jail population on Rikers consisted of everybody being there on felonies. I just want to say that as of yesterday, the population was 6,652 people, 5,652 of which are pretrial, meaning that they are not proven guilty of anything and they are simply there because they cannot afford their bail. 397 of them are there on misdemeanors. 154 of them are there on technical holds. Seven are there on violations, not crimes. Those are not felonies. So I think that's important to have on the record.

Just if I can just say— COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: And– well, no, that's not a question. I'm stating that for the record. I'm going to ask my question now. So I also wanted to follow up on my first round of questioning around on sort of the summonses and the arrests. It

was stated that there were three categories, right? The no ID, which was six percent of those processed arrests, and then the other two categories were if they were want— if they had open warrants, and then the third category was if they were potentially going to be charged with a higher offense. So I wanted to hone in on those second and third categories. That second one, for the— if they had open warrants, how many— how much of the time were those open warrants for other summonses or low-level offenses?

I don't have that data with me, but if someone is wanted on an open warrant, it is our responsibility to return them on it. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Well, okay. So I'm going to say that under the law, under CPL 15020, actually, it says that a DAT is discretionary where there is an open warrant. It's actually the Patrol Guide, not the law, that suggests it's mandatory to take people through a custodial arrest. In fact, under the law, it would be— it would have to be a felony open warrant to make custodial appearance

mandatory. So that's why I want to know how— what the percentage of non-ID arrests include felony charges.

Council Member, just one point on that. It's important. Of course, you're right about 150/20. But here's the thing. If we have someone who we encounter, we know the person has an open warrant, and we just let that person go, we do not return them on that warrant, and that person then goes and commits another crime, hurts somebody after we let the person go on an open warrant, right? We are responsible for what happened. It's a massive liability for the Department and for the city. We cannot do that. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: I will tell you that in my experience as a public defender representing people in court, oftentimes when somebody came through, when they got a summons for sleeping on the subway, for an open container, their open warrant was overwhelmingly usually for another sleeping on the subway or an open container. Not that they were some crazy threat to our safety. So I just– I think that context is important when people are trying to understand actually what it means when

somebody has a warrant, actually what it means when we're spending millions of dollars of resources to police people over these issues while not increasing safety but exacerbating existing problems. So I want to go into that third area of the higher offenses that may be charged. So let's say, somebody is under CPL 15020, eligible for that– an appearance ticket or a desk appearance ticket, and of those higher offenses that you're using the discretion to process, how many of those are for— still under the category of low-level offense? Like, for example, a theft of service. So, like, how many, or the percentage of those that are— you're tracking in that third category are actually other low-level offenses.
We will get you that information. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Okay. Can I ask a few more questions?
Can we go to round three? COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: What’s up?

I promise, Tiffany, I'm sorry. I'll come back to you.

COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: What's up?
I'm gonna come back to you. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: I can't hear you.
I'm gonna come back. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Okay, great. Thank you. As long as you promise to come back.
Okay. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Thank you.
Okay, Council Member Wong followed by Council—

You guys can go. You guys can go. This is going on a long time. I'm going to excuse the executive staff and the people testifying will stay, but we have a lot going on this summer, and I just can't have them staying here all afternoon.
Sure.
Go ahead.
Okay, Council Member Wong followed by Joseph.

Okay, thank you, Chairs. Commissioner, auxiliary police officers were

previously promised bullet-resistant vests after the 2007 murders of auxiliary officers Pacquiao and Marshallik [sp?], with the city committing $3.3 million for vest purchases and recurring support for new members. My question is, is this— is there a recurring baseline budget item in FY 27 for auxiliary police equipment? Because I looked and looked. I just don't see it. So my question is, is there such an item, and that includes vests, radios, and other safety gear?
Deputy Commissioner Ryan will answer that question.
Thank you.

So we did include the request for the equipment for the auxiliary officers as part of our Executive Budget new needs. It was not funded. We will continue to make that request of the Office of Management and Budget.

I see. Thank you. My next question is, Commissioner, I marched in the Israel— excuse me, Israel Day Parade yesterday, and I want to commend the NYPD for the strong security

presence along the route. The police were visible, proactive, and engaged, and the event proceeded without any significant issues. I saw a substantial deployment that included patrol officers, the Strategic Response Group, counterterrorism personnel, and other specialized resources work together to maintain order and ensure public safety. Given some of the large demonstrations we have seen in recent years that have resulted in disorder, property damage, blocked roadways, or arrests, does the success of Sunday's deployment demonstrate the value of a stronger preventive posture, and should the department be utilizing that model more frequently at large-scale protests and demonstrations?

Well, our response to protests and First Amendment activity is governed generally by a settlement agreement entered into a few years ago in the Adams administration. But we look at each event based on the unique circumstances of it, and we design appropriate security packages accordingly.
I see. Okay. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, Chairs.
Okay. Council Member Joseph, then Brewer.
Thank you, Chairs. I have a question around YCO. How many youth coordinators are— do you have within the NYPD?
Hold on. Here we go, I got it. What is it? Can you just answer?
It's approximately 200.
No, we have the exact number.
Yep.
177, thank you. How many officers that are now YCO have pending investigation of abuse and use of force?
We will get you that number.
Thank you. How many young people have YCO arrested or given summons to in the current and last year? And what are the majority charges filed or summons types given to these young people?
We will— we will have to get that— that specific enforcement data to you, because I don't have enforcement broken out by type of officer?
If I could just give a general statement.
Go ahead, give me general, and then I would love to see a breakdown.
Yes, ma'am. The arrests of juveniles is at its highest level for serious crime–
[interposing] Oh, I know.
and we are at our lowest level for low-level crime.
Okay, and you'll–
[interposing] We will get you the specifics.
send me a breakdown of what that looks like?
Yes.
And what are we doing as NYPD and other agencies to combat young people?
Yes.
Thank you.
Thank you. Council Member Brewer, followed by Restler.

Thank you. Also on the youth officers, it's more for me coordination, because the young people leave the high school. Unfortunately, there's a lot of morning smoking, lunch smoking, after-school smoking, etc., in the neighborhood. And the youth officers get stuck with this responsibility, although I think it's more the Department of Education that should be out there talking to the young people. So I've actually tried to get some officers, some people from DOE to go out, et cetera. So my question to you is, because people in the neighborhood complain understandably on their stoop, in the community gardens, and so on. So I guess my question is, what is the coordination between— even though we work at it at the precinct level, I think DOE should be doing more. So I'm just

wondering, at what point do you say to DOE, enough? I mean, this is more of a policy issue than a numbers issue, but it is creating a lot of havoc unnecessarily. I'm just wondering what you think should be the policy there.
You have a thought on this?
Yeah, so I'll just give you general terms again.
Well, I hear— I appreciate it. It's pretty constant.

So we had revamped our Juvenile Crime Strategies Desk to take that— what you're talking about, and make it front and center. And we just had a meeting chaired by the director that oversees the Juvenile Crime Strategies Desk, who is– who's an ex-prosecutor with all the stakeholders when it comes to juvenile crime— DOE, ACS, obviously the prosecutors not only on the family court side, Corp Counsel side, but on the DA's side, on the youth part side. Juvenile probation– it was an outstanding meeting. It was an all-day meeting. I actually went and spoke. So we are really, really trying to focus

on the two sides. The at-risk side, where that is not what we're looking to do as far as arrests. We're looking to— we're looking to visit that family. We call them youths at risk. And then, unfortunately, on the other side, when it comes to violent crime, you know, there has to be consequences. There has to be consequences.
I just want to be kept up to date for how we can work on it together because it's constant.
Yes.
Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you. Restler followed by Banks.

I timed that well. Thank you very much to the Chairs. Thank you again, Commissioner. So the last time I raised this with you, I appreciated that unlike your predecessors, you acknowledge that response times is not— are not where you'd like them to be and are a serious issue, and you're working to improve them. And, you know, we've continued to see– I think in the

most recent MMR, end-to-end response times were 14 minutes and six seconds, up from 10 minutes prior to the pandemic. And most importantly to me, the critical crimes in progress end-to-end, we're looking at nine minutes and 10 seconds, prior to the pandemic, six minutes and 44 seconds. And the times prior to the pandemic had been very consistently in that six-minute-plus range. We're now looking at something that's much higher. There has been some improvement, but we still have a ways to go. Commissioner, what's the plan to address this?

I think it's hiring up to headcount. We need to get the number of people— we— for too many years, the department had authorized headcount and then did nothing with it, meaning didn't hire people to fill those vacancies. And those same people say that it's terrible that we haven't hired 5,000 additional officers. Okay. Separately, I think we are— I am confident that we are going to see the fruits of our hiring of these 4,000 additional officers come to bear starting next fiscal year when they will be in precincts responding to 911 calls for service. Right now, all of these new

rookie officers are doing their first year, 18 months of training on footposts, but they are not in precincts responding to 911 calls for service. And starting in June, we are going to be moving the first tranche of them into those assignments. So, I hope to start to see 911 response time come down as a result.

I appreciate that. And I– you know, you've expressed this to me before, that you think that will make a difference. We saw the end-to-end response times increased by 40-plus percent from pre-pandemic to now. They're slightly down from the worst points in the Adams administration, but still not in a good place. We didn't see a 40 percent modification in headcount. We saw a single-digit percentage modification in headcount. So, could you just help me understand why have things changed so dramatically? Chief, you want to jump in here?

Yes. So unfortunately, you know, the Commissioner hit it when she said lowest level of shootings, murders. But unfortunately, crime is still up 25 percent from pre-pandemic, which means we're responding to a lot

more violent crime than we had in the past. Meaning those complainants, you know, the reports that the officers take, they take a lot of time. They take a, you know– it all starts with a field investigation, and we want good customer service. I want the best of the best customer service. That's what I demand. That's what the Police Commissioner demands. So a 25 percent increase in crime from pre-pandemic means that we are responding to a lot more serious crime, which takes more time to deal with that complaint.
I would love to dig in with this with you further to better understand those trends and what you're seeing and how that is impacting response times.
If I could just make one, one, one real example.
Please.
Let's take—
[interposing] I have 25 seconds. [inaudible]
Let's take [inaudible] up 175 percent from pre-pandemic. That takes a lot of time. Alarm on a car, you know, a lot of paperwork–

[interposing] No, no, I understand. I understand what you're saying. I get it. I would love to dig in with you though and understand where those trends are happening, what types of issues, and what we can do to mitigate them. The last thing I just want to ask, and this is a pet peeve of mine– we have a, I think, global international retailer. I won't shout them out here, but they're from Canada. They're based in our district. They kind of famously have policies that are around no chase, no intervention policy when people steal from them. And so in one of my precincts, three or four commanding officers in a row have made the same staffing decision where they station two cops outside of this business all day, every day. And I— as I understand it, it's for CompStat purposes, that it's to try to reduce the crime that's coming from that business to drive down. And it's just like, for me, I would much rather have those two cops in the heart of downtown Brooklyn rather than standing outside of this business, keeping the whole neighborhood safe rather than doing the bidding, you know, basically working for free.
Well, officers should not be doing– if you're implying that they're doing like private detail—

I'm not. I mean, I think they're functioning as a private detail, but I think that the reason that they're— that three or four commanding officers in a row— so I'm not showing, throwing any specific commanding officer under the bus, that they've stationed them outside of this business is because the business has a no-chase, no-intervention policy on thefts. And so to reduce the number of thefts so their crime stat numbers aren't bad, they just keep two of the officers in front of this freaking store every day.
Chief of Department will talk to you about that.
So, they should not be stationary in front of a store. They momentarily, for, you know, an amount of time—
All day, every day.
I understand.
And you know the business?
I know exactly.
You know who I'm talking about?
I know exactly who you're talking about.
Some people here might [inaudible].
It should be at least a block, a block foot post where those officers walk up and down the block. There are times that they're going to—
[interposing] Inside a mall.

I understand. I'll be [inaudible]. I'm very well versed on it. With, you know, the CompStat, message that you said, I will tell you this. The message from myself, the Chief of Department and all the executives is you did not run your command for CompStat. If you run your command for CompStat, you will no longer be a commander. It's

a process, and the process is at the right place. But I understand your concerns.

I love CompStat. I'm not here to criticize CompStat. I just think that when we're managing toward it, we have problems. I appreciate your comments, and I hope you look into this issue involving this corporation that you know well across the city, because I can't imagine I'm the only one who sees it.
I understand.
Thank you.

Thank you. Okay, so I know we're past, the Commissioner's hard stop time, so, we look forward to hearing— we'll get the rest of members' questions to you and look forward to getting those responses back.
Thank you.
And I just want to say thank you to all of you for being here.
Thank you.

Yeah. Thank you. Thank you so much for being here. Thank you for all the data.

Okay, are you guys ready? Good? On your end, Commissioner? You're good on your end? Okay. Do I just go? All right. Okay. I don't think I need it. Okay, I'll do this just in case. Okay, so good afternoon and welcome to the second FY27 Executive Budget hearing for the day focusing on the Fire Department of New York. I’m Council Member Linda Lee, and I am pleased to be joined by my colleague, Council Member and Chair of the Committee on Fire and Emergency Management, uh, Joann Ariola. Today we have been joined by Council Member Brewer, Council Member Wong, Council Member Paladino, Council Member Banks, and I believe that's it. Okay, so welcome to our amazing FDNY Commissioner and you and your team. And thank you all for joining us today to answer any questions. On May 12th, 2026, the administration released the executive financial plan for FY27 to FY30, with a proposed FY27 budget of $124.7 billion. The FDNY's proposed FY27 budget of $2.67 billion represents 2.1 percent of the administration's proposed FY27 budget in the executive plan, and this is an increase of $23.8

million or 9.9 percent from the $2.65 billion originally budgeted in the FY27 preliminary plan. This increase results from several actions: increased fire prevention staffing funding, 14 new fire inspectors, 84 additional civilian staffing, and an increase of approximately $92 million in EMS projected revenue. As of April 26th, FDNY's headcount was 562 positions less than their fiscal 26 budgeted headcount. In the council's preliminary budget response, we called on the mayor to add $28 million to FDNY in revenue re-estimates in two areas: the foreign fire insurance tax and fire prevention liens. In addition, we called on the administration to address the chronic pay disparity for emergency medical service workers, chronic overtime spending and the ongoing EMS staffing crisis impairing the city's response time. We were pleased to see that our request for the revenue re-estimates were included in the plan, but the issue surrounding pay parity remains to be solved. EMS workers respond to the same life-threatening emergencies as their firefighting colleagues, yet continue to earn significantly less, not just compared to FDNY firefighters, but compared

compared to EMS personnel in virtually every other major city in the country. The result is an attrition crisis averaging nearly 8.3 percent annually, leaving the department perpetually understaffed. The council proposed $50 million in baseline funding to begin closing this gap, and the Executive Budget does not include this investment. I look forward to hearing from the Commissioner on when New York City's EMS workforce can expect to be compensated in a manner that reflects the value of the work that they do. And now I want to turn it over to my co-chair for this hearing, Joann Ariola, for her opening statement.

Thank you, Chair. Good afternoon and welcome to the fiscal year 2027 Executive Budget hearing for the New York City Fire Department. I am Council Member Joann Ariola, and I am Chair of the Committee on Fire and Emergency Management. Today this committee is holding a hearing for one reason, and that is to get answers. We are here to understand whether this budget truly reflects the needs of the brave men and women of the FDNY and whether the promises that have been made to

firefighters, EMS personnel, and the people of the City of New York are being fulfilled. Among the issues we'll examine today are EMS pay increases, the long-overdue implementation of the fifth firefighter, and the status of critical infrastructure improvements throughout the department. For years, our EMS members have been asked to do more with less. They answer hundreds of thousands of calls annually, provide life-saving medical care under extraordinary circumstances, and serve in an indispensable part of our emergency response system, yet they continue to be compensated at levels that fail to reflect the value of their work. We need answers about what steps are being taken to achieve fair pay for these workers and how this administration intends to recruit and retain the next generation of EMS professionals. We will also once again discuss the need for the fifth firefighter on engine companies, which, as we all know, is not a luxury. It is a safety issue. Every second matters in a fire, and every firefighter deserves the staffing levels necessary to perform their duties safely and effectively. The question before us is simple: what concrete steps are being

taken to move this initiative forward? And finally, we must address the condition of the department's facilities. In 2025, the FDNY publicly stated that approximately $940 million had been allocated for capital improvement to firehouses and related infrastructure. Yet, as we review the city's financial plans, many of these projects appear to have been pushed further and further into the out years, in some cases extending through 2035. New Yorkers deserve to know why. Our firefighters are willingly putting their lives on the line every day. They run into burning buildings while others are running out. They work through natural disasters, emergencies, and tragedies without hesitation. They never ask for anything and rarely complain about the conditions they are left with at the firehouse. At the very least the city can do is ensure they return to firehouses that are safe, modern, and fit for the men and women who serve there. No firefighter should be forced to eat, sleep, work in facilities plagued by leaking roofs, apparatus floors ready to collapse, and deteriorating conditions because of long-delayed repairs. Deferred maintenance is not merely a budget

issue. It is a quality of life issue, a moral issue, and ultimately a public safety issue. Today, this committee expects clear answers, clear timelines, and clear commitments. The FDNY is the most respected department in the world. The Fire Department, EMTs, paramedics, and civilian personnel who serve this city deserve an administration that keeps their promises. I would like to thank our committee staff for their hard work: Financial Analyst Tanvir Singh [sp?], Assistant Director Jack Storey, Committee Counsel Josh Kingsley, Policy Analyst Will Hongash [sp?], and my amazing Chief of Staff Phyllis Incirillo [sp?]. I would like to welcome and thank Commissioner Bonsignore and our firefighters, EMTs, paramedics, and the department's civilian staff for the work that you do. I look forward to a candid and productive discussion, and I thank the Commissioner and the Department for the leadership and for appearing here before us today. I would now turn back to Committee Counsel for swearing in.

Okay, just really quickly before we get started, just wanted to remind folks that, we have the executive— all of the

hearings for public testimony on Wednesday, June 10th, beginning at 9:30. So Wednesday, beginning June 10th at 9:30, we are going to have an all-day-long festival for public testimony. So, if you have folks that, you know, want to sign up, please make sure that they do. And with that, I will send it over to our Committee Counsel for swearing in.
